articles.body:
South Africa

The African National Congress came in first place in South Africa's local elections but suffered its worst-ever electoral setback, according to final results on Saturday.

While still the largest party in the country, the once-dominant ANC has won just 32.5% of the vote.

Frustrated voters have turned to the Democratic Alliance, the MK party and other smaller lists.

The ANC's performance marks a drop of roughly 14 percentage points from its 2021 local election results.

The party has failed to win an outright majority in any of the eight metropolitan municipalities. But it finished ahead in four of them, including Johannesburg, Mangaung and Buffalo City.

The centre-right Democratic Alliance is the second-largest party, with about 22.9% of the vote. The party came first in Nelson Mandela Bay and Tshwane, and has secured a majority in Cape Town.

Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party is finishing in third place nationally with around 9.9% of the vote, and came first in the metro of eThekwini.

The results point to a fragmented political landscape. With the results now in, the parties will need to engage in coalition negotiations to form governing alliances.

With outright majorities elusive in several major cities, the results will usher in complex coalition negotiations as parties bargain to assemble the alliances needed to govern.

Such marriages of convenience have often proved unstable, leaving local administrations consumed by internal wrangling at the expense of basic service delivery.

The national government's existing coalition arrangements could further complicate negotiations, political analyst Daniel Silke told AFP.

Voters in Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and the capital Pretoria, would probably prefer to see the DA govern alongside centre-right ActionSA, he said.

"But the animosity between those two parties is extreme."

articles.body:
Australia weakening copyright protections for AI companies would be “ridiculous and dangerous”, the global peak body for the music recording industry has warned as it watches with concern how the Albanese government responds to big tech’s demands.

While local creatives have raised constitutional issues and threatened political backlash, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), representing recording industry bodies worldwide, said its members were worried about Australia potentially agreeing to demands other nations had rejected.

“Why would Australia do this? Why would a sophisticated, democratic country that has a phenomenal cultural power of its own, choose to make this very odd decision and buy into the promises of a few large AI companies, and throw away their own culture and creativity?” Victoria Oakley, the CEO of IFPI, told Guardian Australia.

“I don’t think Australia wants to be the weakest link in this situation, the one that believed the promises and gave in and threw creativity under the bus on behalf of everyone else. That doesn’t feel very Australian to me.

“You just need one safe harbour, because then you can train on music from anywhere in the world. So this isn’t just about Australian music and Australian culture; it’s about music and culture everywhere.”

Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of policy overhauls around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries were alarmed after AI companies requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.

Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model that would allow it to scrape content unless rights holders signalled an objection.

Large AI companies say they need legal certainty on issues like copyright before making investments in Australia or training their models here.

Oakley said AI companies had made similar proposals in the US, UK and other nations and that Australia should not accept such a bargain.

“I just don’t think it’s true that you will only get investment or growth, or be seen as pro-innovation, if you entirely give in to the demands of AI companies,” Oakley said.

“We’ve been talking to capitals around the world, saying ‘are you seeing what’s going on in Australia?’ We think this is a disaster for creativity.”

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said via a spokesperson last week that the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.

Oakley said she worried about AI and copyright “everywhere”, but feared “Australia appears to be threatening to do something really ridiculous and dangerous.”

She said creative industries worried about “contagion” of copyright relaxation if Australia caved in, and that copyright material from anywhere in the world could be affected.

She declined to speculate on any potential legal or constitutional challenges, as raised by the Australian Recording Industry Association, but said it would be reputational damage to Australia’s standing in the creative world.

“It would be a huge mistake, and I think the prize is not worth what you’re throwing away,” she said.

In recent answers to a parliamentary committee on AI, responding to questions from the independent senator David Pocock about why it couldn’t replicate the kind of deals Spotify had made, OpenAI said the music streaming giant “has a different business, where it primarily transmits un-transformed copyrighted content, so would be expected to license content that it streams”.

But Oakley said music labels had already inked dozens of licensing deals with smaller AI companies around the world.

“It is perfectly possible to license. I’m almost shocked that these words are coming out of the mouths of some of the larger AI companies … We already know how to license music to tech platforms because that’s exactly how Spotify works, or Amazon Music, Apple, or Tidal,” she said.

“You have a ready, willing set of rights holders who want to license with a history of licensing in the streaming world, but also current evidence of licensing to AI firms. Let’s let the market do what it needs to do. Come to us and we’ll make it work.”

articles.preview: High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.
articles.body:
The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.

The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”

Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”

But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.

Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”

However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.

Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350.org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”

This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.

However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”

Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.

Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.

Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.

The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”

articles.title: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.summary: Former army chief has 28 days to cobble together a ruling coalition after President chose him over incumbent Netanyahu.
articles.preview: Israel’s former military chief has been given the first opportunity to form a government after an inconclusive election amid deep political divisions. articles.body:
Israel’s former military chief has been given the first opportunity to form a government after an inconclusive election amid deep political divisions.

Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given the opportunity to form a new government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the October elections, raising the possibility of an end to his long tenure in power.

President Isaac Herzog selected the former military chief on Saturday, following consultations with political parties. Eisenkot has 28 days to cobble together a coalition to form a government. If he fails to form a new administration within that period, he can seek a 14-day extension.

“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, posted on X.

However, the 66-year-old faces a difficult challenge as many of the opposition parties hold sharply conflicting positions on national security, religion and the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has a 61-seat majority in Israel’s 120-member parliament, the Knesset.

As a result, Arab-led parties hold a potentially decisive role in determining who governs Israel, even as Eisenkot and his prospective partners refuse to rely on their support.

So what do we now know about Eisenkot’s possible paths to power, and can he succeed in unseating Netanyahu?

Can Eisenkot unite Israel’s divided opposition?

Eisenkot’s potential coalition spans his Yashar party, the centre-left Democrats led by Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett’s centre-right Together party and Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home).

Overall, they control 48 seats, well short of a majority.

Arab-led parties Ra’am (United List) and the Joint List (comprising three parties – Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) – jointly holding 19 seats – have endorsed Eisenkot’s attempt to form a government. Their backing would give the broader anti-Netanyahu camp a combined 67 seats.

Hadash is an Arab-Jewish party, Ta’al advocates for the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Balad demands equal rights for all its citizens.

However, Eisenkot has ruled out bringing Arab parties into his government, while Lieberman has repeatedly rejected forming a minority administration dependent on their support. Golan’s Democrats have been more willing to partner with Ra’am and the Joint List.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan said after the election.

How many seats does Netanyahu’s coalition have now?

Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition has fallen from the 64 seats it secured in 2022 to 53, eight seats short of a majority.

His Likud is the largest individual party with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar won 21.

Netanyahu’s efforts to remain in power suffered a further setback when United Torah Judaism, a longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined to endorse him or any other candidate during consultations with Herzog.

While the decision hurts Netanyahu’s prospects of regaining power, it did not rule out the party supporting him in future coalition negotiations if their demands were met, particularly compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews, which they reject.

What is a minority government?

If Eisenkot is unable to put together a coalition, he could potentially lead a minority government backed by Arab parties from outside.

A minority government is formed when the parties holding cabinet positions do not collectively control a majority of seats in parliament. Instead, they depend on support from lawmakers outside the governing coalition to remain in power and pass legislation.

Eisenkot could establish such an administration with his four-party bloc relying on external parliamentary support from Ra’am and the Joint List.

Under this arrangement, the Arab-led parties would not necessarily receive cabinet positions or formally join the coalition.

They could instead negotiate policy concessions in exchange for their parliamentary support.

In 2021, Ra’am joined a government led by Bennett, becoming the first independent Arab party to participate in an Israeli governing coalition.

That administration collapsed after 18 months, mainly due to disagreements over the illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and Palestinian statehood. Most Israeli parties do not support the creation of a sovereign Palestinian state as part of the so-called two-state solution.

Netanyahu, who has been in power for most of the past 20 years, has openly rejected Palestinian statehood and has pushed settlement expansions that are the biggest hurdles in the realisation of Palestinian statehood. Settlements are considered illegal under international law.

What are the other possible paths to forming a government?

Beyond a minority government, Eisenkot could attempt to secure a parliamentary majority by bringing Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, into his coalition.

Together, they hold 13 seats, which would give Eisenkot’s bloc exactly the 61 seats required for a majority.

However, such an alliance would require compromises over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious students, an issue that has long divided Israeli politics.

Eisenkot and his allies, particularly Lieberman, have criticised the exemptions. But Lieberman has recently indicated that he is open to compromise.

While United Torah Judaism has refused to endorse Netanyahu, Shas backed the beleaguered prime minister.

Another option would be a unity government involving Eisenkot’s Yashar, Bennett’s Together party, Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Netanyahu’s Likud.

Such an alliance would command 67 seats, but would require Eisenkot and his partners to abandon their central election pledge to remove Netanyahu from power.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the required time, Herzog could give Netanyahu an opportunity to form a governing coalition.

Should both leaders fail, parliament could nominate another candidate. If no government emerges after a process lasting 100 days, Israelis could be heading to the polls again.

Why does this matter?

The negotiations could determine not only who becomes Israel’s next prime minister, but also which political parties control key ministries and shape policies on the economy, military conscription and the occupied Palestinian territory.

Several members of Eisenkot’s opposition bloc have previously held senior government positions, including in the coalition that removed Netanyahu from power in 2021.

Bennett, who served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022, has long opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state and advocated annexing large parts of the occupied West Bank.

During Israel’s 11-day war on Gaza in May 2021, Bennett, then an opposition politician, backed Netanyahu’s military offensive in the Palestinian enclave. More than 250 Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks.

Meanwhile, Lieberman served as finance minister in Bennett’s government and previously held the defence portfolio under Netanyahu.

He previously proposed swapping some Arab communities in Israel proper for Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank in the context of a final peace deal with the Palestinians.

Lieberman’s party backs illegal settlement expansion, including E1, and annexing all of Area C, 60 percent of the occupied West Bank already under full Israeli control. E1, which stands for East 1 settlement, is a 12sq km corridor with thousands of housing units. It will cut the West Bank into two parts.

Eisenkot himself served in Netanyahu’s wartime cabinet before leaving the government after disagreements over the conduct of the genocide in Gaza. He has not opposed the genocide but criticised Netanyahu for prioritising his political survival over security considerations.

He has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional”, and he supports “strengthening” illegal settlements.

Academic Neve Gordon says an Eisenkot government could bring notable changes to Israel’s domestic politics, particularly by reversing parts of Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul.

“If Eisenkot is able to establish a government, he will likely be able to stop the judicial overhaul by cancelling the legislation that the Netanyahu government put in place, particularly in relation to the way Supreme Court judges are chosen,” said the law professor at Queen Mary University of London.

Gordon also expects a new government to establish an independent inquiry into the October 7 attacks and potentially introduce legislation preventing politicians facing trial for serious offences from becoming prime minister.

Palestinian citizens of Israel, Gordon said, could also benefit if Arab-led parties support the government from outside the coalition.

“The government is likely to allocate funds to Palestinian towns, adding funds to neglected infrastructures, schools and the like, while also spending more money on policing in order to clamp down on crimes and the high murder rates,” he said.

When it comes to Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, Gordon expects far less change.

“Here the changes will be merely cosmetic,” he said, arguing that Eisenkot’s prospective coalition remains predominantly right-wing and opposed to Palestinian statehood.

Gordon suggested that a new government might attempt to restrain some Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, but questioned whether such efforts would succeed because of the close relationship between settlers and Israeli security forces.

“And I do not foresee any substantial change in policy in the Gaza Strip,” he said.

articles.title: Divided Israelis agree: Forming next government won't be easy
articles.summary: Across Israel people are divided over President Herzog’s decision to pick Gadi Eisenkot to lead country’s next government. But one thing everyone can agree on is that it forming a new government won't be easy.
articles.preview: Israel Across Israel people are divided over President Herzog’s decision to pick Gadi Eisenkot to lead country’s next government. The move was a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who lost his parliamentary majority in last month’s election. But one thing everyone can agree on is that it forming a new government won’t be easy. "I don't know what's going to be, but I want to give a blessing that there should be a new, a new understanding, a new mindset in Israel," says Jerusalem resident Nachman Horowitz.
articles.body:
Israel

Across Israel people are divided over President Herzog’s decision to pick Gadi Eisenkot to lead country’s next government.

The move was a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who lost his parliamentary majority in last month’s election.

But one thing everyone can agree on is that it forming a new government won’t be easy.

"I don't know what's going to be, but I want to give a blessing that there should be a new, a new understanding, a new mindset in Israel," says Jerusalem resident Nachman Horowitz.

"No matter what the government is, no matter what it is, that we should be able to look at one another, be able to respect one another, and that should be instead of focusing on a new government, it should be a new mentality, be able to look at every single person in Israel and be able to come to a new place of respect, of understanding. And that's the biggest thing that I hope will come with no matter what the political situation is.”

Eisenkot didn’t win a majority either. Arab-led parties meanwhile made historic gains leaving them as potential but politically complicated kingmakers.

"What are the challenges you need to overcome? Wow, there are many," says Anny Soronow, another Jerusalem resident.

"First of all, security. Second of all, to protect democracy. Third of all, to reverse the judicial revolution that (Benjamin Netanyahu) Bibi tried to do and then try to work with the with the one Arab party that will join the government hopefully. I have no problem with the Arabs being integrated into the government.”

Eisenkot has six weeks to form a new coalition. It’s a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the 2023 Hamas attacks and three years of war in Gaza and beyond.

articles.title: Tennis world number one Rybakina withdraws from WTA Finals due to virus
articles.summary: Rybakina pulled out on the eve of the Indian Wells tournament, with Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk replacing the top seed.
articles.preview: Rybakina pulled out on the eve of the Indian Wells tournament, with Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk replacing the top seed. Defending champion Elena Rybakina has pulled out of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Finals, saying she was not physically ready to compete, allowing Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk to take her place in the eight-player field at Indian Wells.
articles.body:
Rybakina pulled out on the eve of the Indian Wells tournament, with Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk replacing the top seed.

Defending champion Elena Rybakina has pulled out of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Finals, saying she was not physically ready to compete, allowing Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk to take her place in the eight-player field at Indian Wells.

Organisers on Saturday cited a viral illness as the official reason for the world number one’s “disappointing” withdrawal, but said the world number one needs time to recover from the physical toll of a demanding year.

Tournament director Garbine Muguruza, a former world number one and two-time Grand Slam champion, said she had spoken with Rybakina and that the Kazakh had been unable to recover in time after struggling with physical problems late in the season.

“We love Elena, and we know that she was feeling so-so in Tokyo as well,” Muguruza told the Reuters news agency. “I spoke to her today, and she really couldn’t recover on time.

“What we want is for her to feel good, to go rest, to recover. We don’t want her to feel like she has to play — only if she’s ready to.”

Rybakina, who won two Grand Slam titles this year, also withdrew from the quarterfinals of the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo last month because of a neck injury.

‘Amazing field’ despite Rybakina absence

Rybakina’s absence deprives the event of some star power, but Muguruza said the round-robin format and depth of the field would ensure a high-quality tournament.

“We have the best players,” said Muguruza, who triumphed at the WTA Finals in Guadalajara in 2021.

“I know our world number one is not going to be able to play, but we have an amazing field, the very best,” she added.

“Every match could be a Grand Slam final. You really need to be ready. You cannot give one inch.”

Kostyuk, who is making her WTA Finals debut after a breakthrough season that included the Madrid title and a rise into the top 10, was already in Indian Wells as an alternate and practising when Rybakina withdrew.

Muguruza said the Ukrainian, known for her signature post-match backflip celebrations, had earned her opportunity.

“Marta is great. She’s had a breakthrough year,” Muguruza said. “With this year, we have many first-time players in the Finals, and that’s very exciting. It’s very hard to qualify.”

Kostyuk has been outspoken about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and does not shake hands with Russian or Belarusian opponents. Muguruza said the tournament would support players in making their own decisions.

“They’re free to do whatever they feel,” she said. “We are open and supporting them.”

Opportunity for Sabalenka

Rybakina’s withdrawal could create an opening for world number two Aryna Sabalenka to make inroads in the rankings.

Sabalenka, who won the Indian Wells title earlier this year, has the chance to reduce the gap at the top of the rankings, according to Muguruza, who highlighted Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva as a player comfortable in the California desert.

“Of course, Aryna might be thinking that this can be a good opportunity,” she said.

The WTA moved the finals to Indian Wells from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, with Muguruza saying player safety had been the decisive consideration amid conflict in the Middle East region.

“It clearly felt no longer safe to be in a region where there is conflict,” she said. “Taking care of the players and looking ahead to what could be safe, comfortable and secure, relocating felt the best decision.”

Muguruza said players had responded positively to the switch to Indian Wells, where she competed regularly during her career.

“When we knew that Indian Wells could be the next venue, it was just a joy,” she said, adding that ticket sales have been strong. “The whole thing is just perfect.”

articles.title: Gambia's opposition leader Bensouda files for presidential election despite abuse allegations
articles.summary: Supporters of Gambia’s UNITE-led coalition celebrated on Friday as their party leader Talib Ahmed Bensouda filed his candidacy papers for next month’s presidential election. The move comes despite a government report last week accusing the popular former mayor of financial improprieties.
articles.preview: Supporters of Gambia’s UNITE-led coalition celebrated on Friday as their party leader Talib Ahmed Bensouda filed his candidacy papers for next month’s presidential election. The move comes despite a government report last week accusing the popular former mayor of financial improprieties.
articles.body:
Gambia

Supporters of Gambia’s UNITE-led coalition celebrated on Friday as their party leader Talib Ahmed Bensouda filed his candidacy papers for next month’s presidential election.

The move comes despite a government report last week accusing the popular former mayor of financial improprieties and abuse of office.

Bensouda's UNITE party has rejected the allegations as “a last-minute political manoeuvre intended to confuse the public…ahead of nominations.”

"The NPP government is desperate and afraid because they will lose this election", it said, referring to Barrow's National People's Party.

During his eight years as may of Kanifing Municipality, Bensouda gained a loyal following by implementing regular waste collection. His political star has continued to rise as the tiny west African nation faces prolonged blackouts.

The electricity cuts have led to numerous protests and calls for President Adama Barrow to step down.

The presidential election is scheduled for December 5, when Barrow will be running for a third term. While the list of election nominees has not yet been made official, leading opposition candidate Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, who ran against Barrow in 2021, has also said he will run.

If the allegations against Bensouda are proven, he would be disqualified from standing.

articles.title: Il mare che avanza
articles.summary: When the sea moves in è un progetto collettivo in cui fotografia e ricerca scientifica s’incontrano per raccontare i cambiamenti che stanno ridisegnando le coste italiane
articles.preview: Come si fotografa il mare? Come si può trasformare qualcosa in continuo movimento in un’immagine capace di raccontarlo e renderlo comprensibile? È quello che hanno provato a fare sei fotografi – Fabio Barile, Matteo de Mayda, Giorgio Di Noto, Amina Chouairi, Giulia Parlato e Massimo Sordi– con When the sea moves in, che indaga le trasformazioni delle coste italiane e i fenomeni che ne stanno modificando gli equilibri.
articles.body:
Come si fotografa il mare? Come si può trasformare qualcosa in continuo movimento in un’immagine capace di raccontarlo e renderlo comprensibile?

È quello che hanno provato a fare sei fotografi – Fabio Barile, Matteo de Mayda, Giorgio Di Noto, Amina Chouairi, Giulia Parlato e Massimo Sordi– con When the sea moves in, che indaga le trasformazioni delle coste italiane e i fenomeni che ne stanno modificando gli equilibri. Il lavoro fa dialogare fotografia e ricerca scientifica, ed è articolato in cinque progetti raccolti in altrettanti libri pubblicati da Witty Books.

Le coste del Mediterraneo sono ecosistemi fragili, minacciati dall’erosione, dai cambiamenti climatici e dalle attività umane. L’innalzamento del livello del mare, gli eventi meteorologici estremi, l’urbanizzazione e il turismo di massa stanno modificando il paesaggio costiero, mettendo a rischio non solo gli equilibri naturali, ma anche la biodiversità, le economie locali e il patrimonio culturale.

“Capire questi cambiamenti, ricostruirne le cause e seguirne l’evoluzione nel tempo è indispensabile per immaginare strategie di tutela e interventi di difesa sostenibili”, spiegano Stefania Rössl e Tommaso Parrillo, curatori del progetto. “Non si tratta solo di fotografare ciò che accade lungo le coste, ma di comprendere attraverso quali strumenti possiamo osservare e interpretare le trasformazioni in atto”.

A partire da questa riflessione ogni fotografo ha indagato un tratto del litorale italiano con il proprio linguaggio, concentrandosi su un aspetto preciso. In Atlas undarum Giulia Parlato osserva il mare attraverso esperimenti condotti in laboratorio, in cui il movimento delle onde è riprodotto in scala per studiare il modo in cui l’acqua interagisce con la costa e modifica la distribuzione dei sedimenti. Parlato fotografa questi ambienti trasformando vasche, materiali e movimenti dell’acqua in immagini che nella loro astrattezza a volte somigliano a dipinti. In altri casi realizza still life che rendono visibili processi che di norma lo sono solo per gli addetti ai lavori, mostrando gli strumenti attraverso cui la ricerca scientifica li studia.

Matteo de Mayda e Amina Chouairi in Lagoonal capriccio esplorano il paesaggio poco conosciuto della laguna di Venezia, in particolare le casse di colmata, isole artificiali nate per sostenere lo sviluppo industriale di Porto Marghera e successivamente abbandonate. Attraverso queste immagini, indagano il cambiamento di questi territori nel corso di più di sessant’anni, raccontando un ambiente fragile e in continua evoluzione, segnato dall’erosione provocata dal traffico navale e dalla progressiva trasformazione dell’ecosistema. Ne emerge una visione inedita della laguna, lontana dall’immaginario turistico di Venezia, che invita a riflettere sul rapporto tra esseri umani e natura.

In Layers di Giorgio Di Noto l’attenzione è di nuovo sui processi e sugli strumenti della ricerca scientifica. Il progetto si concentra sulle tecnologie e sui sistemi di osservazione usati per studiare l’erosione costiera, interpretarne i meccanismi e prevederne l’evoluzione.

Nel testo che apre il suo volume Among, Fabio Barile introduce il paesaggio del Lido di Ostia, al centro della sua ricerca, attraverso la descrizione di una scena apparentemente immobile: una superficie marina quasi piatta, lievemente increspata, una spiaggia sabbiosa e un uomo, il signor Array, seduto con le spalle rivolte al mare. Barile invita a osservare gli effetti del tempo sull’ambiente: le onde che consumano gli scogli, la pioggia che scava la pietra. Le sue immagini si concentrano sul progressivo deterioramento delle architetture balneari e sulla loro lenta trasformazione in sabbia, polvere e sedimento.

La serie Rivoluzione di Massimo Sordi prende invece in esame le falesie di Ortona, in Abruzzo, usandole come punto di osservazione del rapporto tra i fenomeni astronomici – come i movimenti dei corpi celesti e le loro interazioni gravitazionali – e i processi che trasformano la superficie terrestre – come l’erosione marina e il progressivo modellamento delle falesie.

Le immagini di questi lavori non formano una narrazione unica, ma costruiscono un insieme di osservazioni che mettono in relazione luoghi e modalità di conoscenza. Pur affrontando temi complessi e spesso molto tecnici, il progetto ha un intento divulgativo: attraverso la fotografia cerca di tradurre fenomeni scientifici in immagini e racconti accessibili a un pubblico più ampio, stimolando una maggiore consapevolezza delle trasformazioni delle coste del paesaggio mediterraneo.

articles.title: Come Cyndi Lauper e i Goonies inventarono gli anni ottanta
articles.summary: Una canzone dimenticata e un film che è diventato un oggetto di culto per generazioni diverse
articles.preview: Rimettendo in ordine i dischi ho ripescato un vecchio 45 giri, uno dei primi che avevo comprato con i miei soldi quando ero ragazzino. Su una facciata c’è una canzone pop confezionata per un film di Hollywood; sull’altra un rockabilly un po’ sgangherato intitolato What a thrill, “che sballo”. Le canta entrambe Cyndi Lauper, una delle popstar più famose della metà degli anni ottanta. Il pezzo sul lato A, The Goonies ’r’ good enough, accompagnava I Goonies, un film d’avventura del 1985 diretto da Richard Donner e prodotto da Steven Spielberg.
articles.body:
Rimettendo in ordine i dischi ho ripescato un vecchio 45 giri, uno dei primi che avevo comprato con i miei soldi quando ero ragazzino. Su una facciata c’è una canzone pop confezionata per un film di Hollywood; sull’altra un rockabilly un po’ sgangherato intitolato What a thrill, “che sballo”. Le canta entrambe Cyndi Lauper, una delle popstar più famose della metà degli anni ottanta. Il pezzo sul lato A, The Goonies ’r’ good enough, accompagnava I Goonies, un film d’avventura del 1985 diretto da Richard Donner e prodotto da Steven Spielberg. Quella canzone arrivò a lambire la Top 10 statunitense: un risultato discreto per un’artista ormai abituata da almeno due anni ai piani più alti delle classifiche pop. Poi, mentre il film cominciava una sua strana vita carsica da oggetto di culto, la canzone scivolava ai margini del repertorio della sua interprete. Fino a finire quasi dimenticata.

Quelle due canzoni (Goonies e What a thrill) sono rimaste incastrate tra She’s so unusual, l’album d’esordio che aveva trasformato Lauper in una star, e True colors, l’album che nel 1986 avrebbe consolidato il suo successo. Nessuna delle due trovò posto in quei dischi. The Goonies ’r’ good enough rimase fuori anche da Twelve deadly Cyns, la sua prima raccolta di successi del 1994. Sarebbe riapparsa in The essential Cyndi Lauper nel 2003, ma ormai era diventata una curiosità laterale: il tema di un film per ragazzi nella carriera di una cantante e autrice di cui perfino un genio indiscusso del novecento come Miles Davis aveva riconosciuto il talento autoriale, incidendo Time after time nel 1985.

Eppure quel piccolo disco dimenticato, con le sue due facciate così diverse, racconta parecchio di Cyndi Lauper. E forse ancora di più degli anni ottanta: anni che le generazioni millennial e post-millennial hanno ricostruito e reinventato riscoprendo e amando anche un film minore come I Goonies.

A metà degli anni ottanta Lauper sembrava fatta apposta per accompagnare una banda di ragazzini un po’ strani, goffi e fuori posto come i Goonies. Anche lei aveva costruito il proprio personaggio di oddball, di eccentrica, mettendo insieme apparentemente a casaccio vestiti da mercatino dell’usato, capelli di tutti i colori, una voce capace di passare dal singhiozzo alla risata, dal cinguettio di un canarino a un registro più alto e pieno, quasi da cantante soul. Perché Cyndi Lauper è sempre stata, a differenza di altre star della sua epoca, anzitutto una cantante. La sua personalità in bilico tra comico e malinconico conservava qualcosa di popolare e sfrontato. E il suo look rattoppato, che univa certe ingenuità hippy a qualche spigolo punk, era pensato per l’estetica frenetica e fluorescente della prima era di Mtv. Nel mondo dei Goonies, dove dei piccoli esclusi diventano eroi di cappa e spada, Cyndi poteva entrare senza neanche cambiarsi. Le bastava essere lei.

La sua canzone, però, che originariamente s’intitolava solo Good enough, non raccontava l’avventura dei Goonies. Era una canzone che parlava di rapporti complicati, aspettative difficili da conciliare con la vita reale. Il ritornello cercava un accordo possibile: quello che va abbastanza bene per te va abbastanza bene anche per me. Insomma: accontentiamoci di quello che abbiamo anche se a volte può sembrare un po’ un casino.

È buffo come certe espressioni tornino a galla nei decenni, ma con significati diversi. Un po’ come i Goonies sono riemersi nell’immaginario collettivo grazie a un bizzarro fenomeno di passaparola intergenerazionale, così l’espressione good enough sarebbe diventata anche una formula tecnologica. Nel 2009 la rivista Wired descriveva la rivoluzione dell’“abbastanza buono”: mp3, chiamate Skype, video compressi e sgranati spesso interrotti dal buffering. Una qualità imperfetta, compensata dalla comodità, dal basso costo e dalla portabilità: “What is good enough for you is good enough for me”, proprio come cantava Cyndi Lauper.

Il suono dell’avventura

L’arrangiamento, con quelle percussioni riverberate e quei tastieroni così anni ottanta, faceva sembrare tutto più semplice. Quel riff di tastiera iniziale che imita il suono della marimba era un facile escamotage sonoro per farci entrare subito nel contesto esotico di un’avventura un po’ da isola del tesoro. Negli anni ottanta il suono del synth che imitava marimba, vibrafoni o gamelan era un suono “finto” che suggeriva un’idea astratta di oriente misterioso: i Japan e David Sylvian lo usavano con classe e poesia in pezzi come Canton del 1981, gli Alphaville in Big in Japan o Murray Head in One night in Bangkok, entrambi del 1984, lo usavano in modo più furbetto ed esotizzante, proprio come lo usava Cyndi in The Goonies ’r’ good enough.

Il titolo della canzone da Good enough e basta fu allungato in The Goonies ’r’ good enough per legarla indissolubilmente al film, con grande irritazione dell’autrice. È per questo che un brano arrivato al numero dieci negli Stati Uniti sarebbe rimasto a lungo ai margini del suo repertorio: era la stessa Cyndi a detestare la canzone e il costosissimo video promozionale che l’accompagnava.

Il video di The Goonies ’r’ good enough era una piccola follia diretta da Donner e divisa in due puntate. Cyndi Lauper, più clownesca e svitata che mai, deve salvare la stazione di servizio della sua famiglia dalle mire di alcuni creditori. Per riuscirci si infila in un’avventura sotterranea, tra pirati e trappole, incontrando i ragazzi dei Goonies e le Bangles, all’epoca pronte a fare il loro grande salto nel mainstream del pop con pezzi come Manic monday e Walk like an egyptian.

I cattivi hanno le facce e i muscoli dei wrestler: tra le varie attività imprenditoriali di Cyndi Lauper in quel periodo c’era anche quella di manager di alcuni lottatori professionisti. Nel video compare perfino il vero Steven Spielberg: Cyndi gli chiede aiuto gridando mentre si trova su un ponte di corda circondata da pirati ed energumeni, ma neanche lui sa come tirarla fuori dai guai. Cinema, Mtv, musica pop e wrestling convergono in uno stesso spettacolo, con l’esuberanza di un’industria che sta scoprendo quanto pubblico si possa raggiungere mettendo tutto insieme nello stesso frullatore.

Sotto tutto quel chiasso c’è una paura concreta. La famiglia di Cyndi nel video è sgangherata, chiassosa, poco presentabile; sembrano tutti usciti da un film di John Waters se mai John Waters avesse fatto film per famiglie. Cyndi sa bene che chi ha i soldi può portarle via il posto in cui vive e lavora. La paura di restare senza nulla è anche il motore del film dei Goonies, i cui protagonisti cercano un tesoro per impedire che le loro case siano demolite per fare spazio a un campo da golf.

In entrambe le storie l’avventura nasce da una minaccia immobiliare. E in entrambe, per difendere la propria vita bisogna diventare ricchi. L’amicizia dà il coraggio di scendere nelle caverne; per fermare i creditori servono i gioielli del tesoro sepolto. Il denaro compra la possibilità di restare dove si è. Insomma, gli anni ottanta concentrati in poche righe di sinossi.

Cyndi Lauper canta dal vivo What a thrill, il pezzo che sarebbe finito sulla facciata B del 45 giri dei Goonies

Alla fine, quegli anni erano proprio questo: la fantasia che un colpo di fortuna possa sottrarti al potere dei soldi degli altri. Riguardando i Goonies e il video di Cyndi Lauper attraverso il filtro della nostalgia, è facile ricordare le biciclette, gli amici e un’infanzia apparentemente libera, lasciando sullo sfondo l’angoscia economica.

I Goonies hanno raggiunto molti millennial attraverso fratelli maggiori, cugini, genitori e videocassette viste fino a consumarle. Il passaggio generazionale era cominciato molto prima di Stranger things, che nel 2016 avrebbe ripreso quella formula di amicizia, pericolo e avventura trasformandola in un nuovo racconto degli anni ottanta. Un nuovo racconto in cui la questione dei soldi rimaneva sullo sfondo ma rimaneva.

“Ma da quando i Goonies è diventato un bel film?”

In Giovani si diventa, un film del 2014 diretto da Noah Baumbach, parlando di un ragazzo che accosta I Goonies a Quarto potere, un personaggio chiede: “Ma da quando I Goonies è diventato un bel film?”. La battuta coglie lo scarto tra un giudizio sul cinema e l’affetto per un oggetto culturale cresciuto insieme a chi lo guarda e custodito come un prezioso ricordo d’infanzia. Per Brian Eggert, che firma un lungo pezzo sui Goonies su Deep Focus Review, rivederlo è “un esercizio di nostalgia avvolto in altra nostalgia”.

Quando Steven Spielberg, nel 1981, girava I predatori dell’arca perduta faceva già un esercizio di nostalgia: si ricollegava a certi fumetti d’avventura della sua infanzia, così come Umberto Eco in quegli stessi anni rivalutava i fumetti degli anni trenta con cui lui era cresciuto e che, come tutti i bambini della sua generazione, era costretto a leggere di nascosto. Gli anni ottanta sono stati anni di cannibalesco consumo d’infanzie perdute: dal grottesco e opulento Flash Gordon del 1980 diretto da Mike Hodges con la colonna sonora dei Queen, al meraviglioso, terribile mondo parallelo di Watchmen creato nel 1986 dal fumettista Alan Moore, in cui i supereroi degli anni quaranta e cinquanta ormai invecchiati non erano riusciti a cambiare né il mondo né se stessi.

The Goonies ’r’ good enough, quel polveroso 45 giri di Cyndi Lauper recuperato facendo le pulizie, è un frammento di questa storia: un decennio che rimasticava le infanzie dei padri per fabbricare quelle dei figli. Questi ultimi avrebbero poi fatto lo stesso, passando ad altri bambini le proprie avventure e trasformando un film di pirati e una canzone pop in ricordi di famiglia. A ogni passaggio qualcosa si conserva e qualcosa si perde. Restano le biciclette, il tesoro, l’amicizia; ma restano anche i debiti, la paura di perdere la casa e quell’idea deleteria della ricchezza vista come premio e come talismano che è forse l’eredità più autentica e problematica degli anni ottanta.

Cyndi Lauper

The Goonies ’r’ good enough/ What a thrill

articles.body:
BEIJING/WASHINGTON/LONDON – China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country.

In fact, the nation’s green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to analysis.

Those loans and grants stemmed from a climate-finance program the world’s wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialized nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis — and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up.

articles.title: US task force to cut off Iran’s transport of advanced weapons: What we know
articles.summary: As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces 'Task Force Iron Gate'.
articles.preview: As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces ‘Task Force Iron Gate’. As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea. With it, the US military is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.
articles.body:
As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces ‘Task Force Iron Gate’.

As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea.

With it, the US military is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.

The same day, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced ambitious plans for underground complexes capable of sustaining missile and drone production under bombardment. That announcement came amid reports of ongoing construction near Iranian missile bases, based on satellite imagery and previous claims by Tehran that US strikes failed to destroy its underground facilities.

Here’s what we know about the US task force:

What is the purpose of the task force?

Task Force Iron Gate will aim to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off” and how “Iran is transporting its energy”, Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

It expands on the US blockade of Iranian ports to cover Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea and will reportedly be run by 20 civilian and military personnel.

Iran shares borders with seven countries – Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan Turkiye and Turkmenistan.

Based in Tampa, Florida, the unit will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM said. Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea”, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

If US President Donald Trump ramps up the war, there will likely be attacks on this “series of targets”, said Mulroy.

“Unlike Operation Epic Fury, which primarily (focused) on military targets, I think these targets will be focused on economic and infrastructure targets, as part of this comprehensive plan to cut the regime off from its ability to fight and ability to fund itself,” Mulroy said. “It’s primarily a coordination body that’s looking for how the US can increase its economic strangulation strategy by going after the ground routes as they’ve already covered a majority of the maritime routes.”

How has Iran responded to CENTCOM’s announcement?

The IRGC dismissed the US military plan as “just a play on words”.

“The Americans cannot achieve their goal through this, which is to apply severe economic pressure to collapse and disintegrate the Iranian economy,” said IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi, as reported by the Fars news agency.

Washington previously “claimed that Iran will suffer an economic collapse within two weeks, but we witnessed that this did not happen”, he added.

Is the task force a response to reports of Russia-Iran weapons ties?

While CENTCOM’s announcement did not explicitly identify Iran’s weapons trade with Russia, analysts say the unit could be seen as an attempt to disrupt supply networks that include Russian connections.

US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea. There are also claims that Russian technology could be helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.

Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of contemporary history and politics at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that reports of military equipment imported via Russia are a “real concern” for the United States.

The task force therefore could “cause a confrontation with Russia”, he said.

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut and a non-resident senior fellow at the Arab Center in Washington, said of the new unit: “The US really doesn’t quite know what to do about Iran as we’ve seen, and it’s doing things off the cuff” – a strategy that has led to little success.

Can the US really choke off Iran’s supply lines?

Khouri pointed to Iran’s history as a trading nation for thousands of years as evidence that the US mission is near impossible.

“There’s an enormous web of contacts that Iran has had for thousands of years with traders and partners and allies all over the region, especially in Asia – it’s virtually impossible for the US to seal off every one,” he said.

While the US can impose a blockade or sanctions on Iran, it cannot control the behaviour of everyone from the Russians, to the Chinese, to the Emiratis and beyond, said the analyst.

“There are people all over the region who have links with Iran, some very close, some just commercial,” he said.

A lot of the materials that go into Iran’s weapons systems are bought from some other countries, – some even from the US or Europeans – and then they are channelled through companies in Asia, Khouri added.

Could this change the course of the war?

Former Trump aide and top counterterrorism official Joe Kent, who resigned in March due to the US’s war on Iran, said the new task force is an attempt by CENTCOM to subvert ongoing diplomatic efforts.

“This is CENTCOM inviting Iran to escalate while the vice president is attempting to negotiate with the Iranians,” Kent posted on X. “This is, as CENTCOM calls it, ‘policy by CONOP’, when the military finds a way to subvert the White House without blatantly disobeying the President, by taking actions that will ensure a war escalates or perpetuates.”

According to The Wall Street Journal, CENTCOM chief Cooper is among the many officials, alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing Trump to renew attacks on Iran.

The task force may also just be symbolic because the US has no military presence on the Caspian Sea, said Zweiri.

“America has no access to the sea, unless some of the neighbouring countries like Azerbaijan or Armenia or others collaborate [with them] … And they’re not collaborating on this because they don’t want to upset Russia,” he said. “It will require … troops on the ground, and this is unlikely to happen.”

Zweiri also said that the Caspian Sea’s contribution to Iran’s economy is just 11 percent, so the task force’s actions won’t have much negative impact on Tehran.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify this figure but the Caspian Sea accounts for only a fraction of Iran’s overall maritime trade, according to the Soufan Center based in New York City.

articles.title: Egypt’s reopening of its embassy in Tripoli signals regional shift on Libya
articles.summary: Former rivals in Libya are pushing for a unity government to end years of conflict.
articles.preview: Former rivals in Libya are pushing for a unity government to end years of conflict. The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated the historic embassy building on Saturday, which had been closed for 12 years due to security concerns. Libya has been politically divided since the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, with rival administrations formed in Tripoli in the west and Tobruk and Benghazi in the east.
articles.body:
Former rivals in Libya are pushing for a unity government to end years of conflict.

The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated the historic embassy building on Saturday, which had been closed for 12 years due to security concerns.

Libya has been politically divided since the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, with rival administrations formed in Tripoli in the west and Tobruk and Benghazi in the east.

Egypt was widely considered to be backing the eastern authority, effectively led by strongman and renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, and his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), until recent regional developments led Cairo to rethink its approach.

Libyan political analyst Hazem al-Rayes said the reopening of the embassy in Tripoli – which was the seat of the internationally recognised government that Haftar was fighting – is a sign of this.

“I can consider that what Egypt is doing in its recent moves towards the capital, Tripoli, is an attempt to readjust its behaviour in the Libyan file … [for] five years, no Egyptian foreign minister visited the capital,” he told Al Jazeera.

Elias al-Barouni, a political science professor at Libya’s Nalut University, also believes the move goes beyond the resumption of regular consular services in Tripoli.

“We are facing an indicator of a shift in Cairo’s method of managing its relations with the Libyan parties, and a rearrangement of its priorities in dealing with the Libyan crisis,” al-Barouni told Al Jazeera.

There have been several significant political and regional shifts that have somewhat stabilised the volatile situation in Libya, where thousands have been killed in fighting between militias attached to rival political authorities.

In July 2026, Ankara and the LNA reached unprecedented coordination, spearheading agreements to develop military facilities, advanced surveillance systems, and training programmes in Turkiye for eastern Libyan officers.

The deputy commander of eastern Libyan forces and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, has also paid visits to regional capitals, including Turkiye and Qatar, which have supported the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli.

In Libya, rivals recently signed the so-called “4+4 agreement” that sets out a roadmap for possible presidential and legislative elections over the next two years.

Badr Hassan al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution at Cairo University, told Al Jazeera that Egypt came to revisit its policy towards Libya after realising that its reliance on eastern forces, led by Haftar, was not conducive to its overall strategic interests.

“It is clear that Cairo … found that relying on one party or leaning towards one party in Libya, which is Haftar’s party, may not be the right bet perhaps at the present time or even for a while, since the Turkish intervention several years ago,” al-Shafei told Al Jazeera.

“Consequently, perhaps Egypt wants to create a balance or also send a message to Haftar that he should not act unilaterally and that acting should be in coordination with Cairo, so it worked to extend bridges of cooperation with Libya also …”

Egypt has also become more concerned about developments to the south of its border, particularly the expansion of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, which had allegedly received support from Haftar.

“Today, Egypt is no longer the Egypt of five years ago when its policies and relations were limited only to the [eastern] authorities in Benghazi,” al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

It is “convinced today that its ally [LNA], which it supported throughout the past years at the expense of the legitimate government in Tripoli … has distanced itself from it today, and it needs to readjust its political behaviour with Tripoli and with the legitimate government”, he said.

Maritime border disputes

During Abdelatty’s visit to Tripoli, he discussed critical economic files with Libyan officials, including the 2019 maritime border memorandum of understanding signed between Tripoli and Ankara.

According to the Facebook page of the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Abdelatty reaffirmed the importance of addressing Egyptian concerns regarding maritime demarcation between Libya and Turkiye in light of international law. The eastern parliament recently ratified the maritime agreement, which it initially opposed.

“Consequently, perhaps Cairo is trying to prevent the ratification of this agreement from causing damage to its interests in gas and oil exploration in the Eastern Mediterranean, and from that it wanted to extend bridges to Tripoli as well,” al-Shafei said.

“Instead of limiting itself to political and diplomatic objection from outside Tripoli, Cairo has become negotiating directly with the Libyan government that signed the agreement.”

Egypt might also be attracted to opportunities that reconstruction and the revival of Libya’s oil industry might bring.

“Perhaps with the reconstruction process, the incoming Egyptian labour will have priority, or even the currently present one will have its living conditions improved, not to mention the idea of the possibility of Egyptian investments and companies entering the reconstruction process,” al-Shafei said.

Push for settlement

After years of backing rival sides, a new regional consensus means there is a greater likelihood of rivals in Libya reaching a comprehensive agreement to end the war, al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

But al-Barouni cautioned that there is still a plethora of issues facing Libya, and only a comprehensive solution can end the divisions within Libya.

“The Libyan problem is not merely a dispute over the name of the head of government, but rather it is a dispute over the nature of power, the distribution of influence, control over institutions and resources, the future of the military institution, and the conditions for reaching elections,” al-Barouni said.

“If Cairo, Ankara, Washington, and other capitals agree on the necessity of ending the division, that is a development that can be built upon, but the success of any settlement remains linked to the ability of the Libyans to formulate an independent national project. Libya needs a settlement that ends the division, not a deal that redistributes the division.”

articles.body:
Second world war veterans outnumbered former prime ministers for what could be the last time at the national service of remembrance at the Cenotaph in central London.

The number of surviving service personel from that conflict attending the service has dwindled from 20 last year to about a dozen, the oldest of whom was Jeffrey Brereton, who served in the RAF. He volunteered for the air force in 1940, at the age of 19, and served as a mechanic on Hurricane aircraft during the Battle of Britain.

The number of former prime ministers has swollen to a record nine, all of whom attended as Andy Burnham took part in the ceremony for the first time. They included John Major, 83, the oldest living former prime minister; Keir Starmer, the most recent ex-premier, and Liz Truss, the shortest-serving.

Some of the spouses of former prime ministers joined Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, on a balcony overlooking Whitehall. She was flanked by Victoria Starmer and Hugh O’Leary, Truss’s husband; Theresa’s May’s husband, Philip; Gordon Brown’s wife, Sarah, and Rishi Sunak’s wife, Akshata Murty.

Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, laid a wreath for the first time. Only leaders whose parties hold six seats or more are entitled to take part, and over the last year defections from the Conservatives have taken Reform beyond that threshold to eight MPs.

Other politicians who laid wreaths included Kemi Badenoch, Ed Davey, Shabana Mahmood and Lindsay Hoyle.

The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, attended the service, with a white peace poppy pinned to his lapel alongside a traditional red one.

The first wreath was laid by King Charles, who was dressed in a field marshal’s uniform. He was joined by his son William wearing the black uniform of a lieutenant colonel of the Household Cavalry.

Minutes before the ceremony, one of the soldiers in the parade on Whitehall was taken away on a stretcher after fainting. Charles led the two-minute silence, which was broken only by a crying baby in Whitehall.

A gun was fired to mark the end of the silence before the Last Post was sounded by the buglers of the Royal Marines. After the service about 10,000 veterans took part in a march-past, with more than 300 different armed forces and civilian organisations represented.

Some veterans waved and saluted as they began the march after the wreath-laying ceremony. Some of the older members were in wheelchairs and one group, many of whom were adorned with medals, rode mobility scooters.

They were applauded by the crowd as they marched swiftly through Whitehall. The youngest person taking part was eight-year-old Ronan Doncaster, who walked in honour of his father, a guardsman with the 1st Battalion Coldstream Guards, who died in April 2024.

In Enniskillen in Northern Ireland, the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, and the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, attended a memorial service. In 1987, the event was targeted by an IRA bomb that killed 11 people on the day and a 12th victim, who never woke up from a coma, years later.

In Scotland, the first minister, John Swinney, led tributes at a service outside Edinburgh City Chambers. A military parade marched down the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle, led by the RAF Central Scotland Pipes and Drums.

A service attended by veterans, faith leaders and representatives of the armed forces was also held in George Square, Glasgow, with a silence at 11am followed by a wreath-laying ceremony.

In Cardiff, the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, became the first leader of Plaid Cymru to lead a wreath-laying at a Remembrance Day service.

articles.title: Poland mourns six killed in attack as authorities launch ‘terrorism’ probe
articles.summary: 'Terrorism' investigation launched after government officials say suspect likely influenced by far-right ideology.
articles.preview: ‘Terrorism’ investigation launched after government officials say suspect likely influenced by far-right ideology. Poland has begun two days of national mourning after an armed man killed six people in central Krakow, as the national prosecutor’s office opened a “terrorism” investigation. The 24-year-old Polish suspect opened fire on Saturday in the heart of Krakow’s historic city centre.
articles.body:
‘Terrorism’ investigation launched after government officials say suspect likely influenced by far-right ideology.

Poland has begun two days of national mourning after an armed man killed six people in central Krakow, as the national prosecutor’s office opened a “terrorism” investigation.

The 24-year-old Polish suspect opened fire on Saturday in the heart of Krakow’s historic city centre. A British national was among those killed, according to police, and nationals from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia were among the 15 wounded, authorities told the PAP news agency.

Three more bodies were later found at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, about 150km (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. Police said they were his parents and a sister.

The suspect was also wounded during police action and is in critical condition in hospital.

Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office said on social media on Sunday it had “launched an investigation today into yesterday’s attack in Krakow”, adding it was probing “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

Daniel Prokopowicz, a spokesperson for the office, said it was “highly likely” that the killings in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski and Krakow were carried out by the same person, but that investigations were ongoing.

According to media reports, the suspect, Michal O, had a valid gun licence and no prior criminal record.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski stated the attacker was influenced by far-right and ultranationalist ideologies and views.

Meanwhile, Krakow’s main market square and the surrounding streets remained closed on Sunday, with police allowing only essential service workers.

Many nearby cafes were closed and flags at the city hall were at half-mast. Mourners placed candles in several locations in the area.

The traditional hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s church on the square was suspended for 12 hours to commemorate the dead, the first time this has happened since 1939, the Polish Press Agency reported.

articles.title: Crash of Indonesian water-bombing helicopter kills crew member
articles.summary: Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.
articles.preview: Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water. JAKARTA: A crew member of a helicopter battling Indonesian wildfires was killed on Sunday (Nov 8) when the aircraft crashed into a river as it scooped up water for an airborne drop, a local disaster agency said.
articles.body:
Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.

JAKARTA: A crew member of a helicopter battling Indonesian wildfires was killed on Sunday (Nov 8) when the aircraft crashed into a river as it scooped up water for an airborne drop, a local disaster agency said.

The crash in Borneo Island's South Kalimantan province was the second in days involving a firefighting aircraft, after a military helicopter plunged into the waters off Borneo on Wednesday, killing three people.

Two Australian pilots survived Sunday's crash and were "safe", Berton Panjaitan, a spokesman for the national disaster mitigation agency, told AFP earlier on Sunday. Further details of their condition were not immediately available.

Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.

"A joint search and rescue team recovered the final victim at 6:08 pm local time during a diving operation involving four divers," a statement released by the search and rescue office in provincial capital Banjarmasin on Sunday evening said.

The Southeast Asian archipelago has been struggling for months to control blazes that have burned through large swaths of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua islands, causing choking haze that drifted to neighbouring Malaysia, East Timor and Singapore.

"This incident occurred while the air fleet was conducting a water-bombing operation," spokesman Berton told AFP.

The Eurocopter EC225LP Super Puma belonged to a company the disaster mitigation agency had contracted for water-bombing operations, he said.

On Wednesday, a helicopter carrying eight people crashed during a mission to fight fires in Tanjung Puting National Park, home to animals including critically endangered Bornean orangutans.

That crash also occurred while the aircraft was scooping seawater for water bombing, according to an army statement that said the cause was under investigation.

Aside from ground-based firefighters, Indonesia has relied heavily on air operations to fight the fires that have destroyed more than 1.9 million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas.

The fires are driven in part by a strong El Nino weather phenomenon, which in Indonesia typically causes drought.

articles.summary: Russian strikes have damaged infrastructure in the Kyiv region and left a kindergarten in ruins in the Ukrainian capital. Firefighters battled a major blaze as Ukraine faced renewed attacks on its energy network.
articles.preview: Footage released by Ukraine's emergency services shows crews directing powerful jets of water towards burning industrial structures, with firefighters working among the wreckage as flames spread through the site. The attacks also damaged energy facilities and a major bridge in Kyiv. articles.body: Footage released by Ukraine's emergency services shows crews directing powerful jets of water towards burning industrial structures, with firefighters working among the wreckage as flames spread through the site. The attacks also damaged energy facilities and a major bridge in Kyiv. In the capital, a kindergarten was left severely damaged, with a large crater in its grounds, shattered walls and children's toys scattered among the rubble. Workers began clearing debris from the destroyed building, while nearby residents inspected the damage. Five people were reported wounded in the strikes. The latest attacks come as Ukraine prepares for another difficult winter, with its energy infrastructure repeatedly targeted by Russian forces. Damage to power facilities threatens to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall, placing further pressure on an already strained network. The renewed bombardment also comes amid diplomatic efforts to bring the war to an end, with talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States under discussion. Despite these initiatives, strikes on civilian areas and critical infrastructure continue, highlighting the challenges facing Ukrainians as the conflict enters another winter.

articles.title: Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
articles.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
articles.preview: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies. Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest. Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
articles.body:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.

Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.

Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.

The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".

Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.

"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.

The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.

Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.

The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.

She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.

Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.

He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.

"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."

Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
