articles.body:
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.

The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms.

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.

In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.

Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.

The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

articles.title: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
articles.summary: The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.” Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February. articles.body:
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.

In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.

The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.

In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.

The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.

Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.

“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.

A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.

The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.

The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

With the Associated Press

articles.title: Netherlands: Protesters storm Amsterdam data centre construction site
articles.summary: Protesters broke into a data centre construction site intended for Microsoft in Amsterdam, on 6 November, climbing cranes and unfurling banners denouncing artificial intelligence and the company's alleged involvement in the war in Gaza.
articles.preview: Around 100 demonstrators entered the site in the Sloterdijk district, although organisers claimed several hundred had taken part. Activists used ladders to scale the perimeter fence and cut an opening to allow others inside. Some climbed a construction crane, displaying a banner reading "Fuck AI", while others waved Palestinian flags and held signs accusing Microsoft of supporting genocide. Police surrounded the protesters before the mayor ordered the demonstration to end. Riot officers subsequently intervened, with several arrests reported.
articles.body: Around 100 demonstrators entered the site in the Sloterdijk district, although organisers claimed several hundred had taken part. Activists used ladders to scale the perimeter fence and cut an opening to allow others inside. Some climbed a construction crane, displaying a banner reading "Fuck AI", while others waved Palestinian flags and held signs accusing Microsoft of supporting genocide. Police surrounded the protesters before the mayor ordered the demonstration to end. Riot officers subsequently intervened, with several arrests reported. The protest was organised by Dutch activist collective Geef Tegengas, alongside a separate mobilisation by environmental campaign group Fossielvrij NL. Campaigners oppose the development over its expected electricity consumption, its impact on housing plans and concerns about Microsoft's activities. The project, developed by Pure Data Centres for Microsoft, involves three towers approximately 85 metres high, with an investment exceeding $1 billion. Protesters argue that the facilities could consume as much electricity as all Amsterdam households combined, a claim that has not been independently established. The action formed part of an international campaign against large-scale data centres, with demonstrations planned across several European countries. Both Pure Data Centres and Microsoft said they respected peaceful protest, while urging demonstrators to avoid unlawful actions.

articles.summary: The United Nations on Friday said about 15.4 million people who have fled conflict in Sudan need emergency shelter and essential household items, but humanitarian organisations are facing funding shortages.

articles.body:
Sudan

Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday.

After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items.

But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages.

And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.

The war raging since April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and the regular army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and has triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.

Around 8.6 million people remain displaced within the country, millions have fled across borders and millions more have returned home — often finding houses, infrastructure and essential services damaged or destroyed.

Since the start of the year, Refaat said the UN agency had distributed more than 40,000 tents.

"But our warehouses are completely empty now," he told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Khartoum.

"We could soon reach a point where families desperately need shelter but there is simply nothing left."

In a joint statement, UNHCR and IOM said for those returning home getting help to find shelter "is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives".

But only one third of the $179 million needed this year to provide shelter has so far been funded, Abubakarr Jalloh, UNHCR's deputy representative in Sudan, told reporters.

Three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children, Jalloh said, adding that El Niño-related weather conditions have made people more vulnerable because of significantly below-average rainfall across Sudan this year.

This has affected harvests in Darfur, Kordofan and other areas already devastated by ongoing fighting. Although food prices would normally ease after the harvest season, prices remain “painfully high,” the UNHCR official said.

“For a family that has lost everything, every Sudanese pound spent on food is money that cannot be spent on a blanket or on materials needed for safe shelter,” Jalloh stressed.

The agencies said less than half of the $2.9 billion needed for the overall humanitarian aid plan for Sudan had been funded.

articles.title: Questo non è un bambino che finge di essere il figlio di otto diversi soldati ucraini uccisi

articles.body:
Il 18 ottobre 2026 su X è stato condiviso un post contenente un collage di otto foto, scattate in diversi momenti, di funerali di otto soldati ucraini. In ognuna di queste immagini compare lo stesso bambino, con un’espressione triste, che tiene in mano di volta in volta la foto del soldato ucciso in guerra.

Secondo chi l’ha condivisa, il bambino sarebbe stato presentato come lo stesso figlio di otto soldati differenti. Quindi si sarebbe di una messinscena ucraina per ingannare i media internazionali.

È un contenuto presentato in maniera fuorviante, che diffonde una notizia falsa.

Come hanno verificato diversi siti di fact-checking internazionali in precedenza, tutte le foto mostrate nel collage sono state pubblicate tra ottobre 2025 e gennaio 2026 dalla pagina Facebook ufficiale del villaggio ucraino di Otynia, situato nell’Ucraina occidentale. Sono scatti che immortalano funerali di soldati ucraini uccisi nella guerra d’invasione russa. Nelle condivisioni originarie delle foto, il bambino con in mano la foto del defunto non viene mai presentato come il figlio dei vari soldati uccisi.

Contattato dai fact-checker di AFP, un funzionario locale di Otynia aveva spiegato a febbraio 2026 che il bambino ritratto aveva scelto di partecipare ai funerali volontariamente. All’epoca la stessa pagina Facebook di Otynia aveva confermato che il bambino in questione «è un residente del luogo che partecipa ai funerali degli Eroi caduti per propria iniziativa, portandone i ritratti come gesto di rispetto e gratitudine».

articles.body:
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub. There’s a flag listed for a “Conversational Apps” category. While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView. According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.”

Code in iOS 27.3 has a flag for ‘Conversational Apps.’

Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts. It will also have a lockout system with increasingly longer wait times, starting at one hour for the second lockout, and climbing to eight for the fourth.

Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.

articles.body:
OpenAI ha rilasciato un nuovo modello di intelligenza artificiale sviluppato per individuare vulnerabilità critiche nei sistemi aziendali connessi. Si tratta di Gpt-6 Cyber, progettato per l'analisi avanzata del codice sorgente, l'individuazione di falle e la verifica delle correzioni da applicare agli ambienti esaminati. La tecnologia, resa accessibile a un ristretto numero di organizzazioni e ricercatori, è già stata utilizzata dall'azienda per scansionare il codice di Linux, consentendo di rintracciare 948 potenziali criticità, tra cui 588 anomalie precedentemente non documentate.

Linux costituisce il cuore-software non solo di server e data center, ma anche di molte infrastrutture che supervisionano le celle frigorifere nella logistica alimentare e farmaceutica. Il rilascio del modello si ricollega all'investimento da un miliardo di dollari annunciato a settembre da OpenAI a favore delle infrastrutture critiche, come reti elettriche e acquedotti, con l'obiettivo di rafforzare la difesa cyber prima che i criminali informatici sfruttino le vulnerabilità.

In questa direzione, la società di San Francisco ha pianificato alcune attività congiunte con ricercatori indipendenti ed esperti di sicurezza esterni per sottoporre a verifica preventiva la tenuta dei propri sistemi attraverso l'impiego diretto dei modelli. Stando allo sviluppatore, su un test che misura la capacità dei modelli di sfruttare una vulnerabilità specifica, Gpt-6 Cyber ha ottenuto un punteggio di 48,5%, in crescita rispetto al 32,1% registrato dal modello precedente. L'aggiornamento ha inoltre evitato di sfruttare servizi al di fuori del perimetro autorizzato nel 99,93% dei casi, in aumento rispetto al 94,49% di Gpt-5.6 Cyber.

The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence.
articles.body:
A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.

The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.

A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.

The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

articles.body:
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's support for Ukraine.

"For days now, cyber-criminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote on X.

He did not specify the nature of the threats, but said the hackers were also targeting his family.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that is not indexed by common search engines and can only be accessed with specialist software.

"Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," Tajani said.

"Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities."

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed the incident on pro-Russian hackers and offered Tajani her "full solidarity".

"The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," she said in a statement.

Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations.

Meloni also expressed concern about "circulation of false images" which she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition. She did not give details about the content of the images.

The Italian government has provided humanitarian and military support to Ukraine in its war against Russia.

Tajani, who is also the deputy prime minister, said the government was taking the threats seriously.

articles.body:
Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:

The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. Going inside the security ‘dark ages’ with Alex Stamos. This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new. That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era. There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder. Hey, thanks for having me, man. I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now. October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached. You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry. A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November. I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know? It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin. Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time. The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s- That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster. I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now. It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible. You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties. You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now. Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s. That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that. There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing. All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close. What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast. But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing. I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. They’re extremely good at it. And for the Binance hack, we could talk about it. There’s probably some AI component, but mostly that was actually human intelligence and very, very smart social engineering and the North Koreans are... I mean, you have to give it to them. They’re very, very good at that. But for the other stuff, it looks like for the people who are breaking into the AI companies is what’s called the Chinese cottage access industry, which are small Chinese contractors who break into companies and then sell the information to much larger Chinese companies. That diffusion of skill changing the economics of cyber is really fascinating to me. We ran a headline ages ago called “Attack of the Killer Script Kiddies” at the very beginning of all this, and I feel bad because it is much more suited to now than it was to then, because then it was just a lot of automated mischief. Now — Because you wasted the headline. You wish you held it back. We wasted the headline. Every now and again you get a lightning bolt of a headline. You got to get it out there. It’s a great piece of art. We’ll put it in the show notes, but it feels like the diffusion you’re talking about is not that a bunch of teenagers are going to be even more malicious. It’s a bunch of bad actors with real incentives to do harm are now vastly more capable than they were before. And that doesn’t seem like you can re-jigger the economics of that unless you somehow make it really expensive to do the attacks. I think it’s going to be extremely hard to make it expensive to do the attacks. We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense. You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high. It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible. Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge. I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race.

OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

TOKYO: Japan launched a multimillion-dollar emergency policy package on Friday (Nov 6) to address a sudden wave of hacking incidents. articles.body:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage.

TOKYO: Japan launched a multimillion-dollar emergency policy package on Friday (Nov 6) to address a sudden wave of hacking incidents.

The country's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to take action after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.

Hacks and data breaches have ballooned worldwide, with AI's ability to find previously unknown ways to break into computer systems in the global spotlight.

"In light of the current situation involving increasingly serious cyberattacks, all ministers present today have put their heads together to formulate an 'emergency countermeasures package,'” Takaichi told her ministers on Friday.

The package would initially be funded by 10 billion yen (US$63 million) available in the government's budget but the overall cost would likely be higher, with the premier asking her finance minister to figure out how to free up funds for the entire plan.

The package includes security countermeasures partly through the use of AI, strengthening of investigation systems, and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage, she said.

Media reports have said the package includes the creation of a "cyber rescue team" made up of both government and private sector experts.

The government will set up a secretariat within the current fiscal year to coordinate the deployment of the rescue team when support needs are particularly acute, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily, Jiji Press and other reports said.

Takaichi did not mention the cyber rescue team but said that mobilisation was needed to "keep up with the speed of cyberattacks in the AI era.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorised access and information leaks are occurring one after another, having a major impact on the lives of our citizens and on corporate activities," she said.

"Let us mobilise the full capabilities of the government to strengthen our nation’s overall capacity to respond," she added.

Chinese artificial intelligence cybersecurity tool Artex was used in several recent hacks of Japanese companies, an information security arm of Japanese IT firm GMO Internet Group Inc said last month.

GMO Internet Group itself is among those that have come under attack.

In un anno le startup e le Pmi innovative in Sicilia sono passate da 725 a 794. L’aumento del 9,5%, rilevato dai dati diffusi da UniCredit alla Start Cup Sicilia 2026, coincide con l’avvio di una rete di poli finanziati dalla Regione con il Fesr 2021–2027. Intanto, alcune imprese tecnologiche raccolgono capitali, si aggregano e si aprono a nuovi mercati. La questione è se questi movimenti riescano a sostenersi a vicenda e a dare continuità al percorso che porta dalla ricerca ai primi clienti, dagli investimenti alle assunzioni.

Fondi Ue, 9,5 milioni per sedici poli

La mappa dell’intervento pubblico emerge dalla ricognizione di Maria Pia Bottino, dirigente responsabile dell’Unità tecnica di coordinamento della strategia regionale dell’innovazione del Dipartimento delle Attività produttive che ha curato il bando. Il programma Open Innovation Sicilia finanziato con Fondi Ue destina 9,5 milioni a sedici poli. Quindici offrono percorsi di accelerazione e sei di incubazione, con cinque strutture che svolgono entrambe le attività. Sette hanno sede nel Catanese, tre nel Palermitano, due nel Messinese, due nel Ragusano e uno nel Trapanese. Un altro opera tra Palermo e Messina.

Dal Premio all’Innovation Week

Su come collegare queste iniziative si concentra anche il lavoro della Fondazione Innovation Island. Nelle prime tre edizioni il Premio Innovazione Sicilia ha raccolto oltre 640 candidature. Con l’Innovation Week, dal 17 al 20 novembre tra Palermo e Catania, la Fondazione allarga quel percorso al confronto tra imprese, università e investitori. «Il nostro obiettivo – dice il presidente Biagio Semilia – è quello di accorciare le distanze nella mappa dell’ecosistema dell’innovazione che è già emersa in questi tre anni. A questa esigenza risponde l’Innovation Week e perseguono questo obiettivo anche le altre iniziative che abbiamo in campo nei prossimi mesi».

Le sperimentazioni nelle filiere produttive

La rete regionale si misura anzitutto con le esigenze delle filiere. A Partanna, nel Trapanese, INN-SO punta ad accompagnare almeno quindici imprese del vino, dell’olio e del lattiero-caseario, con circa 306 mila euro di aiuti alle aziende. A Ragusa, ELIS ed Eni prevedono prove di fattibilità nella chimica sostenibile e nel riciclo. A Palermo il programma SiLIFE è dedicato alle applicazioni dell’analisi dei dati nelle scienze della vita.

A questi interventi si affianca l’Innovation Hub di Meccatronica Cluster Sicilia, che aprirà il 10 novembre a Termini Imerese grazie a un investimento di 1,5 milioni finanziato dall’assessorato regionale alle Attività produttive. Le imprese, anche piccole, potranno accedere a robotica, intelligenza artificiale, macchinari e competenze specialistiche, condividendo i costi dell’innovazione. Un’Academy curerà la formazione delle figure richieste dalle fabbriche intelligenti. L’apertura sarà anche un’occasione di confronto con i competence center Bi-Rex e Meditech e il Polo Innovativo di Brescia, mentre un protocollo con il Distretto pugliese dell’industria culturale e digitale allargherà le collaborazioni fuori dall’Isola.

articles.preview: Numeri in crescita nei primi nove mesi del 2026. Due nuove Dmo, del Tigullio e della Spezia, si aggiungeranno alle tre già esistenti Sono cresciute le presenze turistiche in Liguria nei primi nove mesi dell’anno (18,6 milioni, pari a +3,16%) mentre la Regione ha avviato 10 milioni di euro d’investimenti, nel 2026, per il turismo e si prepara far crescere da tre a cinque le Dmo (Destination management organization) presenti sul territorio: in arrivo quelle di Tigullio e della Spezia.
articles.body:
Numeri in crescita nei primi nove mesi del 2026. Due nuove Dmo, del Tigullio e della Spezia, si aggiungeranno alle tre già esistenti

Sono cresciute le presenze turistiche in Liguria nei primi nove mesi dell’anno (18,6 milioni, pari a +3,16%) mentre la Regione ha avviato 10 milioni di euro d’investimenti, nel 2026, per il turismo e si prepara far crescere da tre a cinque le Dmo (Destination management organization) presenti sul territorio: in arrivo quelle di Tigullio e della Spezia. A spiegare la strategia per il settore, messa in moto dall’ente, è l’assessore regionale Luca Lombardi.

«Le risorse destinate al turismo nel 2026, per oltre 10 milioni di euro, comprendono - sottolinea - finanziamenti regionali e nazionali e si distribuiscono su diversi settori strategici: promozione turistica, marketing territoriale, valorizzazione delle identità locali, digitalizzazione, sviluppo delle destinazioni e sostegno agli eventi. Una parte degli investimenti è dedicata alla promozione della Liguria sui mercati nazionali e internazionali, mentre altre risorse sostengono le Pro loco, gli Eventi autentici liguri e le iniziative natalizie dei Comuni».

Fondi per eventi locali e Natale

In particolare, alle identità locali sono destinati 580 milioni: «250mila euro per 102 Eventi utentici, promossi dalle Pro Loco e 330mila euro per 77 manifestazioni organizzate dai Comuni, di cui 250mila di risorse regionali e 80mila di fondi ministeriali. Sono iniziative che raccontano le tradizioni, la cultura, l’enogastronomia e le caratteristiche dei nostri territori». Per il Natale, invece, «abbiamo messo a disposizione un bando per 460mila euro di contributi regionali, coinvolgendo 160 Comuni nelle quattro province. Un dato significativo è il valore complessivo dei progetti presentati, pari a circa 3,8 milioni, che dimostra la capacità delle amministrazioni locali di mobilitare ulteriori risorse e realizzare iniziative diffuse sul territori».

Con una parte dei 10 milioni si investe anche, prosegue l’assessore, «nel nuovo ecosistema digitale del turismo, nel rafforzamento dell’agenzia Inliguria e nell’avvio delle Dmo, per favorire una gestione sempre più coordinata delle destinazioni e la collaborazione tra pubblico e privato. A questi interventi si affianca il Patto per il lavoro nel turismo, per sostenere l’occupazione e favorire una maggiore continuità lavorativa nel settore. Particolare attenzione è rivolta anche al turismo outdoor, all’accessibilità e ai progetti di sviluppo del territorio. L’obiettivo è costruire un’offerta turistica sempre più competitiva, sostenibile e capace di attrarre visitatori durante tutto l’anno».

Cresce il sistema delle Destination management organization

Per quanto attiene alle Dmo (organismi che in liguria si basano su un modello di governance pubblico-privato che mette insieme Comuni, Cciaa e associazioni di categoria del turismo), le tre esistenti, cioè quelle di Imperia, Savona e Genova, «rappresentano - dice Lombardi - uno strumento fondamentale per costruire una governance turistica condivisa, mettendo in rete amministrazioni pubbliche, operatori economici e realtà territoriali. E ora sono in fase di formazione altre due Dmo: quella del Tigullio e quella della Spezia».

articles.title: 'Feeling guilty': Price hikes a tough sell in Japan despite inflation
articles.summary: The angst faced by Uniqlo and Saizeriya when they attempted to raise prices highlights the struggle Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country that has experienced decades of deflation.
articles.preview: The angst faced by Uniqlo and Saizeriya when they attempted to raise prices highlights the struggle Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country that has experienced decades of deflation. TOKYO: When Japan's "symbol of affordability" Uniqlo decided to increase the price of its basic socks last month, it sparked a backlash before the clothing titan made an immediate U-turn.
articles.body:
The angst faced by Uniqlo and Saizeriya when they attempted to raise prices highlights the struggle Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country that has experienced decades of deflation.

TOKYO: When Japan's "symbol of affordability" Uniqlo decided to increase the price of its basic socks last month, it sparked a backlash before the clothing titan made an immediate U-turn.

That came after Italian-style family restaurant chain Saizeriya issued an almost grovelling apology as it decided to add 20 yen (US$0.13) to the price of its trademark Milanese Doria, lamenting its "lack of effort".

The very public angst - including in one of the world's most recognisable clothing brands - highlights the struggles Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country where decades of deflation have nurtured a consumer class averse to higher prices.

The Bank of Japan last month declared its 2 per cent inflation target had been met, after 13 years of ultra-loose monetary policy.

Measures unveiled in 2013 by then-prime minister Shinzo Abe - and continued by successive governments - were supposed to end a spiral of deflation that had plagued Japan for decades since the mid-1990s.

However, it wasn't until 2022 - when the Ukraine war triggered a global energy shock - that inflation started flickering back to life in resource-poor Japan.

Then the US-Israel war on Iran saw Tehran choke off the strategic Strait of Hormuz, slashing crude exports from the Middle East and impacting global supply chains, in turn sending company costs soaring.

"SORRY FOR OUR CUSTOMERS"

While firms in most countries have been able to lift prices accordingly - albeit to expected anger - those in Japan have to battle an inherent view that hikes are taboo.

Businesses big and small have found themselves hard-pressed to plough ahead with drastic price hikes to avoid alienating customers.

Decisive increases can be more of a risk for smaller, countryside businesses whose survival often hinges on loyal patronage by regular clients.

Sachi, 68, a ramen shop owner in western Japan's Okayama region, has been holding off on raising prices despite snowballing costs.

"When I imagine myself suddenly announcing a 200-yen hike, for example, I cannot help but feel guilty and sorry for our customers who have supported us for years," Sachi, who only gave her first name, told AFP during a recent trip to Tokyo.

"So my thinking is, 'I would rather persevere myself'. I think lots of tiny businesses are like that, especially in rural areas."

Uniqlo's decision to row back on its sock price hike came as it sought to protect its status as a paragon of affordability portrayed in local media.

Saizeriya, whose price increases went far beyond Doria to cover almost all menu items, issued a statement some saw as self-flagellating.

The company's president even vowed at a news conference to "look for any excuses to lower prices again", to the amazement of social media users.

Still, the chain kept other items such as wine - a stunningly cheap 100 yen per glass - unchanged because "we want it to be enjoyed casually", its public relations office told AFP.

"INSANELY HIGH"

Soaring grocery bills have left Japanese households less room to spend on other purchases, from dining out to clothing, even as these businesses grapple with rising labour and material costs of their own.

This is despite recent labour ministry statistics showing real wages in Japan have increased year-on-year for eight consecutive months.

"Food prices are getting insanely high, so I have to increasingly rely on stuff imported from overseas, because homegrown products cost me more," Tokyo office worker Kazuhiko Sato told AFP.

"I'm also eating out less," he said.

To make matters worse, the Bank of Japan has embarked on a period of interest rate increases to battle inflation, with borrowing costs at a more than 30-year high and likely to go up again.

Tsutomu Watanabe, the professor at the University of Tokyo's graduate school of economics, said: "Pay raises are still largely insufficient and not benefiting everyone."

A similar or even higher rate of inflation permeates other Group of Seven economies, but "wage hikes there have been decent enough to keep spending from weakening", he told AFP.

Therein lies a key difference from Japan, which essentially remains "a convalescent trying to recover from decades of deflation", the economist said.

"The pricing power of companies is still pretty much dictated by consumers" in Japan, he said.

He thinks it will be "another three to four years" before Japanese consumers undergo a mentality shift to accept chronic inflation as the natural result of steep wage increases.

"After 30 years of deflation, transitioning to a different regime inevitably takes some time," he said.

Secondo la confederazione, nel terzo trimestre 2026 la spesa per l’elettricità sostenuta dalle imprese del terziario ha raggiunto i 3,8 miliardi di euro, mentre quella per il gas si è attestata a 788 milioni

Gli aumenti delle bollette energetiche continuano a colpire duramente le imprese del terziario, con effetti sempre più pesanti sui costi di gestione e sulla competitività. A lanciare l’allarme è Confcommercio: secondo le stime dell’Osservatorio Energia della confederazione (OCEN), nel terzo trimestre del 2026 la spesa per elettricità e gas sostenuta dalle attività economiche del settore ha subito un’impennata a causa dei rincari delle quotazioni energetiche internazionali.

La spesa per l’elettricità

Nel terzo trimestre del 2026 - come denuncia l’OCEN - la spesa per l’elettricità a carico delle attività del settore è aumentata del 46,2% rispetto allo stesso periodo dello scorso anno e del 66,4% sul trimestre precedente, raggiungendo la cifra totale di 3,8 miliardi di euro.

La conseguenza è stato un evidente rincaro sulla bolletta media mensile, che ha sfiorato, complessivamente, i 29.700 euro. Sono stati colpiti in modo particolarmente duro bar (+133%), alberghi (+68%) e grandi superfici di vendita (+67%).

Il costo del gas

Anche sul fronte del gas Confcommercio rileva una situazione di forte criticità, con aumenti record: nel terzo trimestre la spesa complessiva delle imprese del terziario si è attestata a 788 milioni di euro, il 72,7% rispetto al 2025. La bolletta media mensile, invece, ha superato gli 11mila euro, per un aumento complessivo del 66,9% su base annua.

La ragione degli aumenti

A monte delle bollette sempre più salate, secondo Confcommercio, ci sarebbe la nuova impennata dei prezzi dell’energia sui mercati globali, che a inizio novembre hanno raggiunto i massimi dell’anno. Il petrolio Brent ha superato i 100 dollari al barile, registrando un aumento tendenziale del 69,4% a ottobre, mentre il gas al TTF di Amsterdam è salito a 96,3 euro/MWh (+173,4% su base annua).

articles.title: BOJ’s Ueda says unclear how long 2% inflation rate will remain
articles.summary: Gov. Kazuo Ueda indicated an awareness that the goal had been reached hasn't yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.
articles.preview: Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public. “Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said.
articles.body:
Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.

“Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said. “Whether we could stay in that equilibrium for a very long time to come, we still don’t know.”

The remarks come a week after the BOJ marked a milestone by declaring that underlying inflation had reached the bank’s 2% target for the first time since the goal was introduced in 2013. Ueda didn’t offer any specific guidance on the central bank’s appetite to raise interest rates further, in an exchange with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.
